title: Sample Salary Negotiation Email: 4 Templates That Work
summary: Use these sample salary negotiation email templates to ask for more money professionally. Includes tone tips, customization guidance, and proven scripts.

You've received the offer, you're excited about the role, and then you notice the salary is lower than expected. The recruiter may be waiting for a quick yes, while you're wondering whether negotiating could put the opportunity at risk. A well-written **sample salary negotiation email** gives you a way to respond thoughtfully, protect the relationship, and move the discussion toward a stronger total package.


The email shouldn't read like a closing argument. It should make one clear, evidence-based request and invite a conversation. The templates below show how to do that in different situations, including standard offers, data-supported counters, and compensation packages where the headline salary doesn't tell the whole story.

## The Anatomy of a Winning Salary Negotiation Email


The most important decision happens before you write the first sentence. Treat the message as a **bridge to a structured conversation** , not as an attempt to settle every term in writing.[University of Maryland career guidance](https://careers.umd.edu/find-jobs-internships/offers-salary-negotiation) recommends requesting a call after receiving an offer in writing, while candidates who receive an offer by phone should ask for written confirmation.


That approach changes the tone immediately. Instead of arguing that the employer is wrong, you're showing enthusiasm, identifying a specific point for discussion, and making it easy for the hiring manager to respond. A long explanation can bury your request. A concise message gives the employer something they can take to HR or finance.


### Start with preparation, not persuasion


Before drafting, collect the written offer and separate the package into its components. Look at base salary, bonus conditions, equity, benefits, start date, relocation support, professional development, and the deadline for responding. You need to know whether you're negotiating guaranteed compensation or a figure that depends on performance.


Then choose **one or two priorities** . A request for a higher base salary may make sense when your experience and comparable market data support it. If the base is constrained, a signing payment, earlier compensation review, additional leave, or professional-development support may create a better outcome.


**Practical rule:** Give the employer one clear decision to evaluate, not a list of every improvement you'd like.


Your rationale should focus on relevant qualifications, role scope, market evidence, or measurable business value. Personal expenses may explain why you want more money, but they don't give the employer a professional basis for approving it. The strongest message connects your request to what you can contribute.


### Turn the email into an invitation


A useful structure is simple:


1. Thank the employer and reaffirm your interest.
2. Mention that you've reviewed the offer.
3. State your target or narrow range.
4. Give a concise value-based reason.
5. Invite a short call about the full package.
6. Confirm any agreement in writing afterward.


This is also why email should support, not replace, the conversation. The[salary negotiation email guidance from Acheloa Wellness, Inc.](https://textlauren.com/resources/salary-negotiation-email) offers additional wording ideas for keeping a counteroffer professional and collaborative. For broader career and income planning, you can also explore[Gerald's work and income resources](https://joingerald.com/learn/work--income) .


## Essential Elements and Structure


A strong message follows a deliberate sequence. Each sentence has a job, and removing unnecessary material makes the request easier to approve.


**Subject line:** Keep it recognizable and neutral. “Offer Discussion, \[Your Name\], \[Role\]” works better than a vague subject such as “Question” because it preserves context without sounding confrontational.


**Opening:** Thank the employer and show genuine enthusiasm. Mention the role or team specifically if you can. This establishes that you're trying to make the offer work, not threatening to walk away.


**Review request:** If you haven't received the full package in writing, ask for it before negotiating. If the offer is already written, state that you've reviewed it carefully and would appreciate a short conversation.


**Target:** Name a specific figure or a narrow range based on research. Avoid “something more competitive,” which forces the employer to guess what you mean.


**Value case:** Use one concise sentence about relevant experience, specialized skills, measurable results, or the scope of the role. Two or three quantified achievements can support the discussion, but the email itself should remain easy to scan.


**Package discussion:** Ask whether you can discuss the broader compensation package. Base salary isn't the only lever. Signing bonuses, relocation expenses, professional development, additional leave, flexibility, and review timing may matter.


**Close:** Reaffirm your interest and request a call. The[University of Houston Bauer Career Center's negotiation guidance](https://careercenter.bauer.uh.edu/blog/2023/09/02/moneygeek-guide-negotiating-salary/) emphasizes researched targets, business value, broader compensation, and written documentation of agreements.


A practical version looks like this:


Thank you for the offer. I'm excited about the role. Based on my research and relevant experience, I'd like to discuss a base salary closer to \[target\]. Could we schedule a short call to review the full package?


After the conversation, send a brief confirmation listing the agreed terms. Don't rely on a verbal adjustment that never appears in the revised offer letter.


## Ready-to-Use Email Templates


The right template depends on the quality of the offer and the evidence behind your request. Adapt the bracketed details, but don't leave the message generic. Your target, rationale, and priority should reflect the actual role.


### Standard negotiation template


Use this when the offer is reasonable, but you have a defensible basis for asking for more.


**Subject:** Offer discussion, \[Your Name\], \[Role\]


Hi \[Name\],


Thank you for the offer for the \[Role\] position. I'm excited about the opportunity to join \[Company\] and contribute to \[team, project, or business goal\].


After reviewing the package, I'd like to discuss a base salary closer to \[target\]. My experience with \[relevant skill or responsibility\] and results including \[brief achievement\] would allow me to contribute quickly in this role.


Could we schedule a short call to discuss the salary and the broader compensation package? I'm very enthusiastic about the opportunity and hope we can find an arrangement that works for both sides.


Best, \[Your Name\]


### Data-backed request template


Use this when your market research gives you a clear anchor and your qualifications align closely with comparable roles.


**Subject:** Compensation discussion, \[Your Name\], \[Role\]


Hi \[Name\],


Thank you for sending the written offer for \[Role\]. I'm enthusiastic about the opportunity and the chance to work with \[team or company\].


Based on comparable salaries for similar roles in \[location or market\], and my background in \[specialized skill\], I'd like to propose a base salary of \[target\]. In my current or previous role, I \[quantified achievement\] and \[quantified achievement\], which are directly relevant to the responsibilities outlined for this position.


Would you be open to discussing this figure and the rest of the compensation package by phone? I remain very interested in joining \[Company\].


Best, \[Your Name\]


### Counteroffer for a low offer


Use this when the offer is toward the low end of comparable salaries. The[Interview Pilot guide to pay talks for job seekers](https://www.interviewpilot.app/blog/how-to-negotiate-salary-after-a-job-offer) provides further context on presenting a clear counter while keeping the conversation open.


**Subject:** Offer discussion, \[Your Name\], \[Role\]


Hi \[Name\],


Thank you for the offer for the \[Role\] position. I'm excited about the work \[Company\] is doing and would like to find a way to move forward.


After reviewing comparable salaries for this role in \[location or industry\], I'd like to discuss bringing the base salary closer to \[target\]. My experience in \[relevant area\] and track record of \[specific result\] support that level of compensation.


If the base salary can't move to that figure, I'd welcome a conversation about alternatives such as a signing payment, an earlier compensation review, professional-development funding, or additional leave. Could we speak briefly to review the options?


Best, \[Your Name\]
